### a.

Download the file AUX_I and DEMO_I.

Merge the two files to create a single data.frame. Keep only records which matched.

Print out the dimensions of the merged data.frame.

```{r}
library(haven)
library(dplyr)

AUX_I  <- read_xpt("C:/Users/wl264/Documents/Homework3/AUX_I.XPT")
DEMO_I <- read_xpt("C:/Users/wl264/Documents/Homework3/DEMO_I.XPT")

merged_data <- inner_join(AUX_I, DEMO_I, by = "SEQN")

dimensions <- dim(merged_data)
cat("the dimensions of the merged data (row & column):", dimensions)
```

### b.

Using the following variables. (Gender, Citizenship status, Number of children 5 years or younger in the household, Annual household income)

Clean up each - ensure all missing values are actually NA (rather than 999 or something), and if it’s categorical, convert it to factor with informative levels.

'Annual household income' has an issue with the ordering of the categories here; take a look, identify the issue, and implement a solution.

```{r}
clean_data <- merged_data %>%
  mutate(
    gender = ifelse(RIAGENDR %in% c(1, 2), RIAGENDR, NA),
    gender = factor(gender, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    citizenship = ifelse(DMDCITZN %in% c(1, 2), DMDCITZN, NA),
    citizenship = factor(citizenship, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Citizen", "Non-Citizen")),
    
    children_under5 = ifelse(DMDHHSZA %in% c(0:3), DMDHHSZA, NA),
    children_under5 = as.numeric(children_under5),
    
    income = ifelse(INDHHIN2 %in% c(1:15), INDHHIN2, NA),
    income = factor(
      income, 
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 13, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 14, 12, 15),  
      ordered = TRUE,
      labels = c("0-4,999", "5,000-9,999", "10,000-14,999", "15,000-19,999", "20,000-", 
                 "20,000-24,999", "25,000-34,999", "35,000-44,999", "45,000-54,999", 
                 "55,000-64,999", "65,000-74,999", "75,000-99,999", "20,000+", "100,000+")
    ),
    income = as.numeric(income)
  )
```

### c.

The Tympanometric width measure is looks approximately like a Poisson distribution.

Fit four Poisson regression models predicting a respondent’s Tympanometric width in each ear.

Produce a table presenting the estimated incidence risk ratios for the coefficients in each model, along with the sample size for the model, the pseudo-𝑅2, and AIC values.

```{r}
library(modelsummary)
library(dplyr)

data_1c <- clean_data %>%
  mutate(
    Right_ear = ifelse(AUXTWIDR %in% c(555, 777, 888, "."), NA, AUXTWIDR),
    Left_ear  = ifelse(AUXTWIDL %in% c(555, 777, 888, "."), NA, AUXTWIDL),
    ) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(Right_ear) & !is.na(Left_ear))

# 1R - Right ear: gender
model_1R <- glm(Right_ear ~ gender, family = poisson, data_1c)

# 2R - Right ear: gender, citizenship status (as categorical), number of children (as continuous), annual household income (as continuous)
model_2R <- glm(Right_ear ~ gender + citizenship + children_under5 + income, family = poisson, data_1c)

# 1L - Left ear: gender
model_1L <- glm(Left_ear ~ gender, family = poisson, data_1c)

# 2L - Left ear: gender, citizenship status (as categorical), number of children (as continuous), annual household income (as continuous)
model_2L <- glm(Left_ear ~ gender + citizenship + children_under5 + income, family = poisson, data_1c)

modelsummary(
  list("Right Ear (1R)" = model_1R, 
       "Right Ear (2R)" = model_2R, 
       "Left Ear (1L)" = model_1L, 
       "Left Ear (2L)" = model_2L),
  
  exponentiate = TRUE,  # IRR
  stars = TRUE,         # significant level (*, **, ***)
  fmt = 4,              # Keep 4 decimal places
  
  # N, pseudo-𝑅2, and AIC values
  gof_var = c(
    "Sample Size" = function(x) format(nobs(x), big.mark = ","), # N
    "Pseudo R2"   = function(x) round(1 - (x$deviance / x$null.deviance), 4), # pseudo-𝑅2
    "AIC"         = function(x) round(AIC(x), 2) # AIC
  ),
  
  title = "Estimated Incidence Risk Ratios (IRR) for Tympanometric Width",
  notes = "Exponentiated coefficients (IRR).",
)
```

### d.

```{r}
library(emmeans)
```

Test 1：Likelihood Ratio Test

From model 2L, provide evidence whether there is a difference between males and females in terms of their incidence risk ratio.

```{r}
# Fit a model without gender, then compare it with the full model "model_2L".
model_2L_without_gender <- glm(Left_ear ~ citizenship + children_under5 + income, family = poisson, data_1c)

# Perform a chi-square test to compare the two models
lrt_test <- anova(model_2L_without_gender, model_2L, test = "Chisq")
print(lrt_test)

# Extract the P-value and chi-square statistic for LRT test
lrt_p <- lrt_test$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
lrt_chisq <- lrt_test$Deviance[2]

# Extract the IRR and 95% CI for female compared to male
coef_summary <- summary(model_2L)$coefficients
irr_female <- exp(coef_summary["genderFemale", "Estimate"])
se_log <- coef_summary["genderFemale", "Std. Error"]
ci_lower <- exp(coef_summary["genderFemale", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * se_log)
ci_upper <- exp(coef_summary["genderFemale", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * se_log)
```

Interpretation for test 1： After controlling for citizenship, number of children, and income, the incidence rate ratio (IRR) for women (compared to men) regarding left ear tympanometric width was `r sprintf("%.4f", irr_female)` (95% CI: `r sprintf("%.4f", ci_lower)`, `r sprintf("%.4f", ci_upper)`).

The likelihood ratio test results indicate that including the gender variable significantly improves the model fit (p = `r sprintf("%.4f", lrt_p)`).

Since the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis at the 5% significance level. There is sufficient evidence to indicate a statistically significant difference in the incidence of left ear tympanometric width between males and females after adjusting for other variables.

Test 2：Predicted Values

Test whether the predicted value of Tympanometric width measure of the left ear differs between men and women.

```{r}
# The emmeans package can calculate the predicted means for males and females while holding other covariates at their mean or reference levels.
emm_gender <- emmeans(model_2L, ~ gender, type = "response")
print(emm_gender)
data_emm_gender <- as.data.frame(summary(emm_gender))

# Calculate the difference between male and female predicted values and the p-value
pairwise_contrast <- contrast(emm_gender, method = "pairwise", adjust = "none")
print(pairwise_contrast)
data_pairwise_contrast <- as.data.frame(summary(pairwise_contrast))

male_pred   <- data_emm_gender[data_emm_gender$gender == "Male", "rate"]  
female_pred <- data_emm_gender[data_emm_gender$gender == "Female", "rate"]
diff_est <- data_pairwise_contrast[1, "estimate"] 
diff_p   <- data_pairwise_contrast[1, "p.value"]  
```

Interpretation for test 2：

The predicted mean for men is `r sprintf("%.4f", male_pred)`, and for women is `r sprintf("%.4f", female_pred)`.

The pairwise difference is `r sprintf("%.4f", diff_est)` (p = `r sprintf("%.4f", diff_p)`).

Since p \< 0.05, this provides statistical evidence of a significant difference in the predicted values of left ear tympanometric width between males and females.

### a.

For each store, how many customers does that store have, and what percentage of customers of that store are active in the system?

Method 1: SQL query extract + regular R operations

```{r}
#' method1_a
#'
#' @returns A data.frame containing the store ID, total customers, active customers, 
#' and the percentage of active customers.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
method1_a <- function() {
  df_a <- dbGetQuery(sakila, "SELECT store_id, active FROM customer")
  
  res <- df_a %>%
    group_by(store_id) %>%
    summarise(
      total_customers = n(),
      active_customers = sum(active == 1),
      active_percentage = (active_customers / total_customers) * 100
    )
  return(res)
}
```

Method 2: single SQL query

```{r}
#' method2_a
#'
#' @returns A data.frame containing the store ID, total customers, active customers, 
#' and the percentage of active customers.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
method2_a <- function() {
  a2 <- "
    SELECT store_id,
           COUNT(*) AS total_customers,
           SUM(CASE WHEN active = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS active_customers,
           (CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN active = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / COUNT(*)) * 100 AS active_percentage
    FROM customer
    GROUP BY store_id
  "
  res <- dbGetQuery(sakila, a2)
  return(res)
}
```

Compare each method using microbenchmark

```{r}
kables(
  list(
    kable(method1_a()),
    kable(method2_a())
  )
)

# microbenchmark
bench_a <- microbenchmark(
  SQL_Extract_R_Process = method1_a(),
  Single_SQL = method2_a(),
  times = 50
)
print(bench_a)
```

### b.

Generate a table identifying the names and country of each staff member.

Method 1: SQL query extract + regular R operations

```{r}
#' method1_b
#'
#' @returns A data.frame containing three columns: first_name, last_name, and country.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
method1_b <- function() {
  staff <- "SELECT first_name, last_name, address_id FROM staff"
  addr <- "SELECT address_id, city_id FROM address"
  city <- "SELECT city_id, country_id FROM city"
  country <- "SELECT country_id, country FROM country"
  
  df_staff <- dbGetQuery(sakila, staff)
  df_addr <- dbGetQuery(sakila, addr)
  df_city <- dbGetQuery(sakila, city)
  df_country <- dbGetQuery(sakila, country)
  
  res <- df_staff %>%
    left_join(df_addr, by = "address_id") %>%
    left_join(df_city, by = "city_id") %>%
    left_join(df_country, by = "country_id") %>%
    select(first_name, last_name, country)
  
  return(res)
}
```

Method 2: single SQL query

```{r}
#' method2_b
#'
#' @returns A data.frame containing three columns: first_name, last_name, and country.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
method2_b <- function() {
  b2 <- "
    SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, co.country
    FROM staff s
    JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
    JOIN city c ON a.city_id = c.city_id
    JOIN country co ON c.country_id = co.country_id
  "
  res <- dbGetQuery(sakila, b2)
  return(res)
}
```

Compare each method using microbenchmark

```{r}
kables(
  list(
    kable(method1_b()),
    kable(method2_b())
  )
)

bench_b <- microbenchmark(
  SQL_Extract_R_Process = method1_b(),
  Single_SQL = method2_b(),
  times = 50
)
print(bench_b)
```

### c.

Identify the name(s) of the film(s) which was/were rented for the highest dollar value. (Assume all costs are in USD regardless of country.) (Hint: You can merge a table more than once.)

Method 1: SQL query extract + regular R operations

```{r}
#' method1_c
#'
#' @returns A data.frame with one row containing two columns: the film 'title' 
#' and its 'total_revenue'.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
method1_c <- function() {
  pay <- "SELECT rental_id, amount FROM payment"
  rent <- "SELECT rental_id, inventory_id FROM rental"
  inv <- "SELECT inventory_id, film_id FROM inventory"
  film <- "SELECT film_id, title FROM film"
  
  df_pay <- dbGetQuery(sakila, pay)
  df_rent <- dbGetQuery(sakila, rent)
  df_inv <- dbGetQuery(sakila, inv)
  df_film <- dbGetQuery(sakila, film)
  
  res <- df_pay %>%
    inner_join(df_rent, by = "rental_id") %>%
    inner_join(df_inv, by = "inventory_id") %>%
    inner_join(df_film, by = "film_id") %>%
    group_by(title) %>%
    summarise(total_revenue = sum(amount)) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_revenue)) %>%
    slice(1) 
  
  return(res)
}
```

Method 2: single SQL query

```{r}
#' method2_c
#'
#' @returns A data.frame with one row containing two columns: the film 'title' 
#' and its 'total_revenue'.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
method2_c <- function() {
  c2 <- "
    SELECT f.title, SUM(p.amount) AS total_revenue
    FROM payment p
    JOIN rental r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
    JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
    JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
    GROUP BY f.film_id, f.title
    ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
    LIMIT 1
  "
  res <- dbGetQuery(sakila, c2)
  return(res)
}
```

Compare each method using microbenchmark

```{r}
kables(
  list(
    kable(method1_c()),
    kable(method2_c())
  )
)

bench_c <- microbenchmark(
  SQL_Extract_R_Process = method1_c(),
  Single_SQL_Query = method2_c(),
  times = 20 
)
print(bench_c)
```

### d.

In Australia, phone have 10 digits, they write land lines and cell phones differently1:

Landlines: 12-3456-7890

Cell phones: 1234-567-890

Make all phone numbers written like cell phones.

Show it works by printing the first 10 phone numbers of each column.

```{r}
#' format_cellphone
#'
#' @param phone A character vector containing phone numbers.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of the same length as phone, containing the 
#'   formatted phone numbers in the cell phone pattern.
#' @export 
#'
#' @examples format_cellphone(au$phone1)      format_cellphone(au$phone2)
format_cellphone <- function(phone) {
  digits <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", phone)
  
  paste0(
    substr(digits, 1, 4), "-",
    substr(digits, 5, 7), "-",
    substr(digits, 8, 10)
  )
}

au$phone1_new <- format_cellphone(au$phone1)
au$phone2_new <- format_cellphone(au$phone2)

cat("phone1 (first 10):\n")
print(head(au$phone1_new, 10))
cat("\nphone2 (first 10):\n")
print(head(au$phone2_new, 10))
```

### f.

Benford’s law is an observation about the distribution of the leading digit of real numerical data. Examine whether the apartment numbers appear to follow Benford’s law. Do you think the apartment numbers would pass as real data?

```{r}
first_digits <- substr(as.character(apt_clean), 1, 1)

actual_prop <- table(first_digits) / length(first_digits)

benford_prop <- log10(1 + (1/1:9))

comparison <- data.frame(
  Digit = factor(1:9),
  Benford = benford_prop,
  Actual = as.numeric(actual_prop[as.character(1:9)])
)
comparison$Actual[is.na(comparison$Actual)] <- 0

barplot(
  t(as.matrix(comparison[, c("Benford", "Actual")])),
  beside = TRUE,
  names.arg = 1:9,
  col = c("lightblue", "pink"),
  legend.text = c("Benford", "Actual"),
  args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n"),
  main = "Benford vs Actual Leading Digits",
  xlab = "Leading Digit",
  ylab = "Proportion"
)
```

The actual first digits of apartment numbers do not conform to Benford's Law. According to Benford's Law, the digit "1" should appear most frequently (approximately 30%). As the digits increase from 1 to 9, their frequency should decrease monotonically. However, the actual data shows a completely different trend: the digit "1" accounts for only about 10%, while larger digits such as "9" occur at a much higher rate than expected—reaching approximately 15%. Therefore, these apartment numbers cannot be treated as numeric data. And, because these data do not conform to Benford's Law, making it difficult to pass the Benford's Law test as real data.
